extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of formal logic, philosophy, and classification theory
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and practical guidance for forming and describing classes (genus, species, differentia, proprium, accidens) and for writing definitions; explains when classifications count as 'real kinds' versus convenient or accidental groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: The five Predicables (genus, species, differentia, proprium, accidens)
rubrics_metrics.description: General names (predicates) may be classified into five relative kinds — genus, species, differentia, proprium, accidens — not by their own meaning but by the relation their denoted class bears to the subject on a particular occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these five categories to analyze how a predicate relates to a subject; remember they are relational (the same name can be genus, species, or differentia depending on the subject). Examples: 'animal' is a genus with respect to man, a species with respect to 'substance'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus and Species (popular vs. logical senses)
rubrics_metrics.description: In popular use, any class including another may be called a genus or species (e.g., Animal/Man). In the Aristotelian/logical sense, genera and species are 'real Kinds' distinguished by an indeterminate multitude of properties, not merely by a finite or superficial difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between casual, convenience-based classifications and those corresponding to 'Kinds' where the difference pervades many (possibly unknown) properties. Avoid treating every subdividable aggregate as a logical species when its distinguishing differences are merely finite or derivative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infima/Proximate Species
rubrics_metrics.description: The proximate (infima) species of an individual is the lowest real Kind to which it is referable; the properties common to that proximate Kind necessarily include the common properties of any larger Kind the individual belongs to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When identifying the proximate species, ensure it comprehends (known or unknown) properties of all broader Kinds applicable to the individual. Use this to determine correct hierarchical placement: every other predicable will be a genus relative to the proximate species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentia (specific difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: The differentia is the part of the connotation of a species-name that distinguishes that species from all other species of the same genus — i.e., the surplus of connotation that must be added to the genus to complete the species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiae can be ordinary or technical (special connotation) and may vary with the purpose of classification (e.g., naturalists may use different differentiae than common parlance). Example: 'rationality' is the traditional differentia of 'man' relative to 'animal'; but a naturalist might instead use dental or locomotion characters as the differentia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentia depends on classificatory principle and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: A species’ differentia is not fixed by nature alone but may be chosen according to the principle or practical purpose governing the classification; the same nominal species can connote different differentiae in different classificatory contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about the classificatory aim when assigning differentia (scientific convenience may justify different criteria). Avoid confusion by noting when a term acquires a technical connotation for the purposes of an inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proprium (properties that necessarily follow but are not connoted)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proprium is an attribute belonging to all individuals of a species which, though not part of the name's connotation, follows necessarily from the connoted attributes — either demonstratively or causally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize two kinds of proprium: (1) follows by demonstration (logical consequence from connoted predicates), (2) follows by causation (effect consequent on an essential attribute). Example: opposite sides equal is a proprium of parallelograms (demonstrative); capacity to understand language follows from rationality for man (causal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidens (accidents) — separable and inseparable
rubrics_metrics.description: Accidents are attributes neither connoted by the name nor known to follow necessarily from connoted attributes. Inseparable accidents are universal in existing experience but not necessary in principle; separable accidents are actually absent in some individuals or times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify observed attributes as inseparable (e.g., blackness of crows in current knowledge — universal but not essential) or separable (e.g., color of Europeans, being born, being in a place). Avoid treating inseparable accidents as part of connotation or essence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unlimited power to form classes (but meaningful vs. arbitrary classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: One may form classes on any detectable difference — classification power is unlimited — but there is an important distinction between classes distinguished by a finite/determinate property (often arbitrary or purposive) and those distinguished by an inexhaustible series of properties (real Kinds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use practical convenience to justify certain classifications, but acknowledge when such divisions do not correspond to logical 'Kinds'. Prefer classifications that reflect pervasive, law-governed differences when the aim is to discover natural groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotation as the ground of Differentia/Proprium/Accidens distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinctions between differentia, proprium, and accidens are not grounded in nature but in what is connoted by the name (either ordinary or technical). The classification of an attribute depends on whether it is part of the connotation, follows from the connotation, or is unrelated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the connotation (explicit or specially assigned) of terms before assigning attributes to one of the predicables. Be cautious of metaphysical 'essences' — these distinctions are linguistic/semantic rather than ontological facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical (special) connotation of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Words may acquire special technical connotations in scientific or classificatory contexts that differ from common usage; such special connotations become part of the meaning for that context and can serve as differentia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using a term as a term of art, explicitly state the technical connotation (e.g., define 'man' for a particular taxonomic scheme by specific dental or anatomical characters). Failing to note special connotation risks equivocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition as a proposition declaring meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition is a proposition that declares the meaning of a word — its connotation for connotative names — or states what the speaker/writer intends to annex to a word in a particular discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the direct form ('X is a name connoting such and such attributes') for precision, though it is verbose and technical; the indirect form (predicating other known names) is customary and briefer. Ensure definitions align with the classification scheme in use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper names are not definable
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper names lack connotation (they are mere marks for individuals) and therefore cannot be defined in the sense of declaring connotation; descriptive propositions about a proper name only indicate reference, not definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attempting to 'define' proper names by attributes; instead indicate reference (e.g., 'John Thomson, son of General Thomson') while noting this is not a definition of the name's meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practices for choosing definitions and differentiae
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions should declare the connotation intended in the discourse; where direct precision conflicts with brevity, use indirect predicate-names but remain unambiguous. Differentiae should be selected according to classificatory goals and made explicit when technical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the classificatory purpose and any technical senses prior to defining terms; be consistent in usage to avoid equivocation. Recognize and document when ordinary meanings are supplanted by technical connotations.
